questions.q: How do Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules differ from traditional antivirus signature scanning?
options: ASR rules are identical to antivirus signatures, just renamed by Microsoft
ASR rules only scan email attachments and have no effect on running processes
ASR rules only work on Windows Server, never on Windows 10 or 11 workstations
ASR rules block specific malicious behaviors (like Office spawning a child process) regardless of which malware family is attempting it, rather than matching known-bad files
questions.explain: ASR targets the handful of behaviors malware commonly relies on, which is why a rule keeps working against malware families that didn't exist when the rule shipped.

questions.q: What does the real ASR rule 'Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem' specifically stop?
options: All outbound network traffic from the machine
The kind of lsass.exe memory access that Mimikatz-style credential dumping relies on
Office applications from opening any file at all
Users from changing their own passwords
questions.explain: This rule blocks the specific memory-access pattern credential-dumping tools like Mimikatz use against lsass.exe.

questions.q: What is the purpose of running a new ASR rule in Audit mode before switching it to Block mode?
options: To see what the rule would have blocked without actually blocking it, so legitimate business processes can be identified and excluded before enforcement begins
Audit mode only applies to Windows Server, not workstations
Audit mode is required by Microsoft licensing and has no technical purpose
Audit mode permanently disables the rule so it never takes effect
questions.explain: Audit mode logs what a rule would have blocked (Event ID 1125), letting a team find and exclude legitimate processes before ever enforcing the rule.

questions.q: What does Event ID 1125 indicate in the Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational log?
options: Windows Defender itself crashed
A rule actually blocked an action in enforced Block mode
An ASR rule in Audit mode would have blocked an action, but did not actually block it
A new ASR rule GUID was just published by Microsoft
questions.explain: Event ID 1125 is the audit-mode equivalent of Event ID 1121, which logs an actual block once a rule is enforced.

questions.q: In the lesson's rollout example, how did the team handle the one legitimate business process the ASR rule would have blocked?
options: They disabled Windows Defender across the whole organization
They added a targeted exclusion for that specific file/process, confirmed it during a second audit pass, then switched the rule to Block mode fleet-wide
They ignored the audit findings and enabled Block mode anyway without any changes
They abandoned the ASR rule entirely rather than risk breaking anything
questions.explain: A scoped exclusion for the one verified-legitimate process let the team enforce the rule everywhere else without an outage.
